definition: Stymie means to block the progress of an effort so completely that it stalls, leaving no clear way forward.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stymie. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stymie should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The detectives were stymied for weeks: the vault had been emptied, yet every lock was still sealed from the inside, and each new lead went nowhere.
Hinder is milder than stymie: a hindered effort is slowed — detours, setbacks, lost time — but it still inches forward, while a stymied one has stopped dead with no way ahead.
Thwart is stronger than stymie: a stymied plan is stuck and can still revive if the obstacle clears, while a thwarted plan has been defeated outright — that attempt is finished.

To obstruct is to place a barrier in the way — a road, a view, or a process can all be obstructed, and the word describes the barrier, not the outcome. Stymie reports the result: the effort has actually stalled, stuck with no clear way forward until something changes.

To baffle is to defeat the mind — a baffled person cannot understand what they face. Stymie defeats the effort itself: a stymied team may see the obstacle with perfect clarity and still be unable to get past it.
to make a process easier and help it move ahead
to push a plan or effort forward

On the green, a player was stymied when an opponent's ball lay dead in her line; today the passive form is everywhere — negotiators are stymied by a veto, researchers are stymied by missing records — and it is the shape of the word you will most often meet on the page.
Stymie means to block the progress of an effort so completely that it stalls, leaving no clear way forward.

The city's plan to uncover the buried creek was stymied by a single missing utility map — until it turned up, no crew could dig an inch without risking the gas lines that ran somewhere beneath the park.
Stymie says more than 'slowed' and less than 'defeated': a stymied effort is not destroyed, it is stuck — halted at a standstill until something changes.
The missing map does not doom the creek project or merely delay it; it freezes the work in place, with the goal still visible and no safe way to move toward it.
vivid and slightly informal; at home in news reporting
Stymie is the newsroom's word for gridlock: bills are stymied in committee, mergers are stymied by regulators, and the word usually arrives in the passive — plans are stymied by something.

This unit hands you its nearest neighbors, and they divide the work cleanly: hinder only slows an effort that keeps moving, and forestall stops trouble before it ever starts, while stymie catches the effort already underway that has run into a wall and stalled.
In formal prose, 'obstruct' or 'block' will do; stymie adds the golfer's exasperation — so near the hole, and no way through.

The bypass was designed, funded, and staked out by the spring of 2019; engineers called it the easiest route the county had ever drawn.
Then the project met Ellen Marsh, whose forty acres sat squarely across the only grade the trucks could climb.
She would not sell, the courts upheld her deed, and for six years the finished plans sat in a drawer -- the whole effort stymied by one signature that never came.
There was no confusion about the problem.
Every engineer could point to the exact fence line where the road stopped; understanding it changed nothing.
Work resumed only when a new survey found a longer grade to the north, and the county quietly bought its way around the obstacle it could never move.
